_comment: spec-v593 section 2 exception class: metric that IS US trade practice. Each entry waives check-us-defaults findings whose label contains `match` in `module` (module "*" = any). Additions are reviewed like citations, against the section-2 acid test: would a US tradesperson read this number in this unit off their own instrument, code table, or product label? Every entry must waive at least one finding no other entry already waives: on 2026-09-04 seven did not (four matched a token combination the scanner can never produce, three were subsumed by a broader entry in the same module) and were removed.

entries.justification: mg/L is the universal US water-ops unit (SDWA/SWTR reporting, jar tests, MLSS).
SV30 settleometer reads mL/L on the cone itself.
Sludge Volume Index (SVI) is universally reported in mL/g in US wastewater ops (Standard Methods, WEF, operator-certification exams); there is no US-customary equivalent.
CT tables (SWTR) are published in mg-min/L.
Peak ground / seismic acceleration in g (gravity), not grams: ASCE 7 and USGS publish in g.
entries.note: grams collisions are covered by module-scoped lab/kitchen entries

entries.justification: ICEA P-32-382 conductor short-circuit limits are published in deg C.

Module-wide: US lab practice is SI throughout (mL, uL, mg, g/mol, M, g/mL, cm cuvette paths, mm rotors). Spelled "*" since 2026-08-30; it was an empty string, which exempted the module by accident rather than by decision.
Baker's percentage and equilibrium-cure recipes are written in grams in US kitchens.
UTM easting/northing are defined in meters (USGS quads print meters).
UTM easting/northing are defined in meters.
TIA-568 defines the 90 m permanent link / 100 m channel in meters.
TIA-568 cord budgets are specified in meters.
Fiber attenuation is specified in dB/km on every datasheet.
Grain-size and sieve-opening diameters are stated in mm by ASTM D2487 / D6913 and printed in mm on every US geotechnical gradation report; there is no US-customary equivalent in use.

Permeameter tests (ASTM D2434 constant head, D5084 falling head) are run in metric in US geotechnical labs: sample length, standpipe/burette heads, and mold dimensions are read in cm off the apparatus, and hydraulic conductivity k is reported in cm/s universally. There is no US-customary equivalent in lab practice.
Camera sensor formats and lens focal lengths are sold in mm.
Lens focal lengths are sold in mm.
Metric thread pitch is the product spec on the box.
Metric thread pitch is the product spec on the box.
The tile's metric-thread entry path; US pitch field sits beside it.
Brake pad thickness is published and measured in mm in US shops.
Pad wear-rate shop data rides the mm pad-thickness convention.
Wheel offset is stamped ET in mm on the wheel itself.
LED panel pixel pitch is sold in mm.
Module datasheets publish record temps and coefficients in deg C.
Cell/ambient temperature model inputs are datasheet deg C.
NOCT is a datasheet deg C value.
Power temperature coefficients are datasheet %/deg C.
Peak-sun-hours insolation data is published in kWh/m2/day (NREL).
Plane-of-array irradiance is published in W/m^2.
Spore-trap lab reports count spores per cubic meter.
Air-sampling pumps are calibrated in L/min.

SCBA breathing/consumption rate is expressed in L/min: NIOSH rates open-circuit SCBA duration at 40 L/min and NFPA 1981 heavy-work testing at ~103 L/min, and US fireground air-management training teaches ~40 L/min light / ~100 L/min heavy. There is no US-customary breathing-rate unit a firefighter reads off the rating.
Sampling cassette volumes are specified in liters.
Soil particle density is quoted in g/cc (2.65) in US soils practice and every geotech lab report.
ACI 318 minimum-thickness span ratios l/20..l/28 (l = span), not liters.
Span ratio result line (l = span), not liters.
IEEE Std 80 step/touch equations take the crushed-rock layer hs in meters as published.
US beverage bottles are labeled in mL (750 mL).
Loan Estimate section C (services you can shop for), not Celsius.
SWTR CT tables are published against deg C water temperature.
lightning-countdown secondary metric output line; the primary Distance (mi) output line precedes it -- the sanctioned US-primary + metric-secondary pattern.

free-space path loss is metric-native: the Friis constant 32.44 is defined for km and MHz, and RF engineering (including US practice) states link distance in km and frequency in MHz; there is no US-customary form of the FSPL equation in common use.

Fresnel-zone radius is metric-native: the 17.32 constant (sqrt(300)) is defined for km and GHz, and RF path surveys state distances in km; no US-customary form of the Fresnel-zone equation is in common use.

Settling-particle and grit sizes are stated in mm and micron in US water/wastewater and environmental-engineering practice (grit-chamber and sedimentation design, the same ASTM grain-size convention already allowlisted for calc-earthwork D10/D30/D60); there is no US-customary equivalent for a particle diameter.
The motor nameplate itself marks temperature rise in °C, and NEC 430.32(A)(1) states its 40 °C threshold in °C. The tradesperson reads this number off the nameplate in this unit.

Gobo and gate sizes are specified in millimeters everywhere in the US entertainment-lighting trade: an M-size gobo is 66 mm outside diameter with a 48 mm image, and every US manufacturer's catalog and every fixture's spec sheet prints those figures in mm. A US lighting technician reads this number in mm off the gobo holder itself.

Radiant heat flux is expressed in kW/m2 everywhere in US fire-protection engineering: the SFPE Handbook, NFPA standards, and every published ignition and tenability threshold state it that way, and a US fire protection engineer reads the number in that unit off their own reference.

The t8/5 weld cooling-time model has no US customary formulation: EN 1011-2 and every welding-metallurgy reference write it in kJ/mm, degrees Celsius, and millimetres, and a US welding engineer computing it reads those units off the procedure and the literature. Converting the inputs would make the tile disagree with every published worked example of the model.

ISO 1940-1 defines the balance grade itself in millimetres per second and the permissible unbalance in gram-millimetres per kilogram, and a US balancing machine's readout is in those units. A US shop balancing a rotor enters mass in kg and the correction radius in mm because the standard and the machine both do; converting would make the tile disagree with the readout.

Rolling-element bearings are metric worldwide including in the US: a 6310 IS 50 x 110 x 27 mm, and the bore, outside diameter, and width are the designation itself and are stamped on the bearing. A US millwright reads these numbers in millimetres off the part in their hand.

The ICEA P-32-382 conductor short-circuit temperature limits, and the insulation damage temperatures they are compared against, are published in degrees Celsius -- the same basis the catalog's existing conductor short-circuit withstand tile is allowlisted on. A US electrical engineer reads the 75 C and 250 C limits in Celsius off the standard itself.

The ICEA P-32-382 conductor short-circuit temperature limits, and the insulation damage temperatures they are compared against, are published in degrees Celsius -- the same basis the catalog's existing conductor short-circuit withstand tile is allowlisted on. A US electrical engineer reads the 75 C and 250 C limits in Celsius off the standard itself.

Atomic weight has no customary-unit form at all -- it is grams per mole by definition, and it is the value a plater reads straight off the periodic table or the bath supplier's data sheet to enter Faraday's law. Converting it would produce a number that appears in no reference a US plating shop owns.

Plating and metallurgical references list metal density in g/cm3 universally, including the ones on a US plating shop's shelf, and it pairs directly with the g/s mass rate Faraday's law produces. A US plater reads 8.9 for nickel off that table; lb/cubic ft would have to be converted back before it could be used.

A metric COMPANION to the primary US output: the same tile prints "Blend (lb/acre)" directly above it, and kg/ha is how agronomic rate recommendations and fertilizer research are published. US-first with a metric sibling, not metric-defaulted.
A metric COMPANION: the haversine tile prints "Distance (miles)" directly above it. Aviation and marine plots read both, and the cited Earth radius is given in mi and km.

RTD (IEC 60751 Callendar-Van Dusen), thermistor Beta, and Steinhart-Hart curves are DEFINED in degrees C -- the coefficients have no Fahrenheit form -- and every one of the three tiles prints "Temperature (°F)" on the next line. Verified 2026-09-04 when output labels were first scanned.
